Index Accuracy – Measure of performance for categorical predictions; percentage of correct predictions out of total attempts (p.176–178). Adjacency list listing each node along with the nodes it connects to and the weight of each edge (p.32, 50–52). Algorithm designed to perform a specific task, such as sorting a list (p.139–140). • Algorithm performance – Evaluation of how efficiently an algorithm runs, often measured by execution time in best-case and worst-case scenarios (p.72–74). • Algorithms (data structures) – Sets of instructions that control data structures, defining rules for size, data type, and operations (p.33). Artificial General Intelligence (AGI / General AI) that could learn and apply intelligence flexibly across many tasks, similar to humans. Not yet achieved (p.217, 236). Associations – Links formed between known and new information; essential for learning (p.158–159). Array (List) – A linear data structure that stores items sequentially in memory. Arrays have a fixed size and homogeneous data type: items can be updated but not inserted or removed (p.12–13, 33–35). Bar chart categories are represented by bars; useful for comparing quantities across categories. Can be vertical or horizontal (p.15, 17, 19). Bias – An ethical concern where AI reproduces unfair patterns from biased training data, leading to unequal treatment (p.228–229). Best-case scenario – The situation in which an algorithm finds the target immediately or completes its task with the fewest possible steps. For example, in search, it may succeed on the very first item checked (p.73, 85). Big Data – Large datasets characterized by volume and variety; improve AI models by helping them generalize and make more accurate predictions (p.184). Binary search – Search algorithm for sorted datasets that repeatedly divides the search range in half until the target is found or eliminated (p.75–79). • Flowchart – Diagram showing binary search process (p.77). • Pseudocode – Step-by-step outline of binary search (p.79). • Execution time – Grows logarithmically with dataset size, modeled with log (n) (p.80–82). • Requirements – Dataset must be sorted (p.75, 86). Black box problem and decision-making where systems lack transparency, making it difficult to explain or challenge outcomes (p.223). Block that performs a task, usually part of initialization, main body, or termination (p.140). Bubble sort – Sorting algorithm using the strategy of pair, compare, and swap. Repeatedly passes through the list, swapping adjacent items if out of order (p.111–113, 117–123). • Process – Uses outer loop (repeats passes) and inner loop (compares/swaps adjacent pairs) (p.117–123). • Pseudocode – Instructions for bubble sort (p.120– 123, 153). • Performance – Requires more steps than insertion sort; poor scalability; inefficient for large datasets (p.134–138). Categorical data – Another name for qualitative data, which can be grouped and labeled but not measured (p.18). Categorical prediction – Prediction task where the AI classifies inputs into categories (e.g., cat or not a cat, language detection) (p.175–176). Charts – Visual tools to present data. Four common types: line chart, scatter plot, bar chart, and pie chart
Appendix (p.14–15). Child node – A node that descends from a parent node in a tree structure (p.46). Cleaning data – Removing erroneous or implausible data values before processing (p.12). Continuous data – Quantitative data that can take any value within a range (e.g., temperature, height, time). Best visualized with line charts or scatter plots (p.16–17). Continuous learning – The idea that learning does not stop after training; models can keep improving with new data and feedback (p.165). Continuous prediction – Prediction task where the AI estimates a numerical value (e.g., house prices, rainfall, travel times) (p.178–180). Control and Robotics direct machines acting in the physical world. Applications include self-driving cars, industrial robots, delivery drones, robotic surgery, agricultural robots, and disaster-response robots (p.226–227). Criterion (sorting) – The basis for sorting, such as numeric (scores, prices, time) or alphanumeric (names, book titles) (p.95). Data – Raw values or signals that can be processed into meaningful information (p.8). Data structures – Methods of organizing data in computers, such as lists (arrays), tables, stacks, queues, trees, and graphs (p.12–13). • Dynamic size – Property of structures like lists, stacks, and queues that allows them to grow or shrink as items are added or removed (p.34, 39, 42). Decision-making – The process of selecting the best choice from several options by weighing their outcomes and choosing the one with the highest utility (p.197–200). Discrete data – Quantitative data that can only take whole-number values (e.g., number of students). Often visualized using bar charts (p.17). Edge – A link between two nodes in a graph, often carrying additional information such as distance or latency (p.32, 50–52). Error – The difference between predicted and actual values; can be positive (underestimation) or negative (overestimation) (p.180). Ethics and responsibility – Principles ensuring AI respects human rights, fairness, safety, privacy, and accountability, while reducing risks of harm or inequality (p.228). Execution time – The time required for a program to complete its run. • time per attempt × number of attempts (p.72, 80–82). • step count and memory latency (p.124–125, 131–133, 138). Explanation – Reasoning backward from an observed outcome to uncover its most plausible causes, contributors, or relationships (p.201–204). FIFO (First In, First Out) – Principle governing queues; the first item added is the first removed (p.42–44). Flow & control – Flow is the sequence of steps in a program; control refers to conditions that determine which steps are executed, repeated, or skipped (p.139). General AI – see Artificial General Intelligence (AGI). Given outcome that serves as the starting point for explanation (p.201– 202). Graph – A non-linear data structure where nodes can connect freely to represent complex relationships. Edges may store additional information (p.32, 49–54). Hierarchy – Organizational model in which data items are arranged at levels, such as in a tree structure (p.31, 45–47). Hold index / hold data – Variables in sorting algorithms representing the index and the value temporarily stored for comparison (p.103, 116). Information – Data that has been processed into meaningful form, typically through identification, organization, visualization, and interpretation (p.8–11, 21). • Interpreting data – The final step; answering “why” and “what should we do?” to make data actionable (p.20–21).
Index • Labeling data – Adding descriptive identifiers (e.g., “temperature, outdoor, Celsius”) to clarify meaning and context (p.11). • Organizing data – Arranging data to make it usable, through cleaning, structuring, or sorting (p.11–13). Inference piece of information by linking premises (facts, observations, or predictions) into a conclusion (p.195–197). Initialization – The first block of a program, where variables are declared and initial values assigned (p.106–107, 119–120). Insertion sort – Sorting algorithm using the strategy of compare, shift, and insert. Builds a sorted section one item at a time (p.99–106, 139–140). • Process – Uses outer loop (moves through each index) and inner loop (compares/shifts until correct position is found) (p.103–106). • Pseudocode – Instructions for insertion sort (p.106–110, 152). • Performance – Fewer steps and faster than bubble sort; still scales poorly for very large datasets (p.124–130). Job displacement human workers without retraining opportunities, leading to unemployment and inequality (p.229). Knowledge base – The collection of rules, facts, and learned patterns that reasoning processes rely on to connect conditions to outcomes (p.201). Labeling data – see Information. Language (AI cognitive function) – Natural Language Processing (NLP) enables AI to analyze, interpret, and generate human language. Applications include translation tools, chatbots, large language models, sentiment analysis, and educational tools (p.220–221). Leaf node child nodes (p.46). Learning – The ability to form and use new associations; requires pattern recognition, association, and repetition (p.158–159, 166). LIFO (Last In, First Out) – Principle governing stacks; the last item added is the first removed (p.39–41). Linear search – A simple search algorithm that checks each item in order until the target is found or the end is reached (p.68–71). • Flowchart – Diagram showing linear search process (p.69–70). • Pseudocode – Step-by-step outline of linear search (p.71). • Execution time – Grows linearly with dataset size (p.72–73). • Applicability – Works on both sorted and unsorted datasets (p.75, 84). Linear structures – Data structures where items are stored sequentially: array, list, tuple, stack, queue (p.33–34). List – A linear data structure with dynamic size, accepts mixed data types, and allows insertion or removal at any position (p.36–37). Logic – The rules that guide reasoning from premises to conclusions; the framework for inference, decision- making, and explanation (p.194). Logarithmic growth – Growth pattern of binary search execution time; efficiency improves as dataset size increases (p.80–82). Loop – Control structure used to repeat a set of instructions. Sorting algorithms use outer and inner loops (p.104–106, 117–122). Machine learning computers are designed with learning capabilities to identify patterns, form associations, and improve through repetition (p.159). Mean Absolute Error (MAE) – A measure of performance for continuous predictions; the average size of errors regardless of direction (p.180–183). Memory latency – Delay between requesting data from memory and receiving it; becomes significant for large datasets stored outside cache (p.131–133, 138–139). Misclassification model incorrectly labels or classifies input data (p.163–164, 176–177). Model – The internal system that represents recognized patterns, labels, and rules about what features matter or don’t (p.162–163).
Natural Language Processing (NLP) – AI technology that processes, translates, and generates human language in text or speech (p.220). Narrow AI designed to perform small set of tasks very effectively (p.216–217). Node – A data construct used in trees and graphs to store both data and links to other nodes (p.46–48, 50). Order (sorting) – Direction in which data is arranged, e.g., ascending (least to greatest) or descending (greatest to least) (p.95). Parent node – A node with child nodes branching structure (p.46). Pattern recognition – The ability to detect recurring regularities, such as the shared shape of cups regardless of color or design (p.160). Pie chart – A circular chart showing categories as slices of a whole, indicating proportions or percentages (p.15, 20). Plausibility reasonable or believable an explanation is, based on how well its premises fit the observed outcome (p.201, 204). Prediction (or humans) estimates the most probable outcome based on learned patterns (p.174–175). Prediction & Forecasting – AI’s ability to analyze past data to estimate future outcomes. Applications include finance, healthcare, meteorology, retail, education, sports, and urban planning (p.224–225). Premises – The starting points of reasoning; can be facts, observations, predictions, preferences, or rules (p.195, 197–198). Privacy – An ethical issue involving AI misuse of personal or sensitive data without consent (p.229). Program instructions a computer can execute to run an algorithm (p.139). Qualitative data – Descriptive, categorical data that can be observed but not measured (e.g., gender, grade levels, types of cars). Must often be converted into quantitative form for visualization (p.18–19). Quantitative data – Data that can be measured (continuous) or counted (discrete). Best visualized with line charts, scatter plots, or bar charts (p.16–17). Queue – A linear data structure that follows FIFO. Items are added at the end and removed from the beginning (p.42–44). Reasoning thinking to discover, decide, or explain. Outcomes may be inference, decision, or explanation (p.194, 206). Reasoning and Decision-Making (AI) – AI’s ability to evaluate options and select actions in a specific domain. Examples include recommender systems, logistics planning, dynamic pricing, and game-playing AIs (p.222–223). Repetition – Strengthens associations and improves pattern recognition in both humans and AI (p.158–159, 166). Root node – The topmost node in a tree structure from which all other nodes descend (p.46). Scalability – How an algorithm’s performance changes as dataset size increases. Sorting algorithms like insertion and bubble sort scale poorly due to quadratic growth (p.129–130, 137–138). Scatter plot – A chart showing individual data points, often used to highlight relationships or correlations between two variables (p.14, 16–17). Search index – Position within a dataset being checked during a search algorithm (p.71, 78). Search range still under consideration in a binary search; updated each iteration (p.78). Searching – Fundamental operation required to locate a specific item in a dataset before modification, extraction, or processing (p.68, 83). Sorting – The process of arranging data in a specific order based on a criterion, such as chronological order, increasing or decreasing value, or categories. Sorting makes it easier to search, interpret, and analyze data (p.13–14, 94–98). Stack – A linear data structure that follows LIFO. Items can only be added or removed from the end (p.39–41). Step count – The number of operations an algorithm performs. Used alongside execution time to measure performance (p.124, 126–127, 135). Supervised learning learning that uses labeled data; the system is trained with examples Appendix
where the correct answer is provided (p.160). Swap – Operation in bubble sort where two adjacent items exchange positions. Each swap requires three moves in memory (p.135). Table rows and columns; well-suited for organizing multiple sets of related data (p.12–13). Termination – The final block of a program where a message indicates the task is complete and the program ends (p.110, 123). Training – The process of improving a model using new data and corrections. It involves analyzing mistakes, refining rules, and updating the model to improve accuracy and generalization. Effective training depends on both the volume (amount) and variety (diversity) of training data (p.163–165, 178, 183–184). Transparency and accountability – Ethical principle requiring AI decisions to be explainable and challengeable. Lack of transparency creates risks of unfair or harmful outcomes (p.229). Tree – A non-linear hierarchical data structure with nodes connected along branches, including root, parent, and child nodes (p.31, 45–48). Tuple – A linear data structure with fixed size and format, can store multiple data types together as a unit (p.37–38). Uncertainty – The degree to which reasoning outcomes may not be definite, especially when based on predictions or incomplete premises (p.197, 204– 205). Underestimation/Overestimation – When predictions consistently fall below or above actual values (p.180–182). Unsupervised learning learning that uses unlabeled data; the system identifies patterns and groups similar items without predefined labels (p.161). Utility useful, valuable, or goal- fitting an outcome is; used to evaluate decisions (p.200). Visualization – Presenting data in visual form (charts, graphs) to highlight patterns and trends (p.14–15). Worst-case scenario – Situation where an algorithm must check all possible items before concluding, or in sorting, when data requires the maximum steps (e.g., reversed order for ascending sort). Represents the longest possible execution time (p.73–74, 124–127). Index
